titre: The Day Surgery Stopped Making People Scream
accroche: On October 16, 1846, in Boston, a patient does not scream while a tumor is removed from his neck, a first in public
contenu_vulgarise:
On October 16, 1846, in the surgical amphitheater of Massachusetts General Hospital in Boston, known today as the Ether Dome, the surgeon John Collins Warren is about to remove a vascular tumor from the neck of Edward Gilbert Abbott, a young printer. A dentist, William Thomas Green Morton, places over his face a glass inhaler containing a sponge soaked in ether.

## An Operation Without Screams

Before this day, surgery is practiced without reliable anesthesia: speed is the surgeon's only weapon against pain, and amputating a leg in under thirty seconds is considered an honorable feat. A year earlier, in this very amphitheater, the dentist Horace Wells had tried to demonstrate the virtues of nitrous oxide on a patient who began to moan in the middle of a tooth extraction; the demonstration ended amid cries of “Humbug!” (hoax).

This time, Morton has Abbott breathe the ether for three to four minutes, until he loses consciousness. Warren makes the incision: the patient does not react. On waking, Abbott describes a mere scratching sensation. Legend has it that Warren then turned to the audience and declared: “Gentlemen, this is no humbug,” but no written account reports this sentence before 1859, thirteen years later.

## A Discovery No One Can Hold Back

The news crosses the Atlantic in a few weeks: by December 1846, European surgeons are already operating under ether. In the space of a single season, anesthesia becomes a worldwide medical advance, irreversible, and immediately reproducible by anyone with ether and an inhaler.

## The Price of Claimed Glory

What shifts our view of this story is not the discovery itself but what follows. Morton, Wells, and the chemist Charles Jackson, who had suggested to Morton that he use ether, dispute the paternity of the invention for decades, each claiming all the credit. Wells sinks into experimenting with vapors on himself, is arrested in New York for throwing acid at passersby, and kills himself in prison on January 24, 1848. Morton dies on July 15, 1868, in New York, ruined by the legal costs of his ether patent, after a collapse following his reading of an article crediting Jackson with the discovery. Jackson is committed in 1873 and dies in a psychiatric asylum on August 28, 1880.

Since then, anesthesia has relieved hundreds of millions of patients, and none of its three main claimants gained either fortune or peace from it. The value of a discovery and the fate of the person who claims it can follow entirely independent paths.

repere.texte: The sentence that history attributes to Warren, “Gentlemen, this is no humbug,” appears in no written account before 1859, thirteen years after the events, in a biography of Morton written to support his claim for financial compensation. The only eyewitnesses to report it speak only in 1896, fifty years later.
repere.source: Haridas RP, “‘Gentlemen! This Is No Humbug’: Did John Collins Warren, M.D., Proclaim These Words on October 16, 1846, at Massachusetts General Hospital, Boston?”, Anesthesiology, 2016, vol. 124, no. 3, pp. 553-560

carte.punch: The sentence that made this day famous was probably never spoken.
carte.idee: On October 16, 1846, in Boston, a patient does not scream while a tumor is removed: the first successful public anesthesia. The sentence that history attributes to the surgeon Warren appears in no account before 1859, thirteen years later.

quiz.question: Why does Wells's demonstration in 1845 fail while Morton's in 1846 succeeds?
choix: Wells used an ineffective gas, while Morton's ether was the only anesthetic known at the time
Wells operated without the consent of the chief surgeon, which discredited his method
Wells's patient did not receive a sufficient dose of nitrous oxide and reacted to the pain
The 1845 public refused, on principle, the idea of painless surgery
quiz.explication: Nitrous oxide is a real anesthetic, but the dose Wells administered was insufficient: the patient moaned, which discredited the demonstration. Ether was not the only gas known, Wells's operation did have the hospital's approval, and the public of the time was, on the contrary, actively looking for a solution to surgical pain.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What do we know about the sentence “Gentlemen, this is no humbug,” attributed to Warren?
choix: It was noted the same day by a witness present in the amphitheater
It appears in no written account before 1859
It was spoken by Morton, not by the surgeon Warren
It appears in the operating register kept by the Boston hospital
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The phrase is attested only thirteen years after the events, in a biography of Morton written to support his claim for financial compensation. The only eyewitnesses to report it speak only in 1896, fifty years later: it is very probably apocryphal.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What role does the chemist Charles Jackson play in this story?
choix: He had suggested to Morton that he use ether
He himself made the incision on the patient
He had led the failed demonstration of 1845
He publicly renounced any claim
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Jackson had advised Morton to use ether, which served him as a basis for claiming paternity of the discovery for decades. The incision was Warren's, the failed demonstration of 1845 was Wells's, and far from renouncing, Jackson disputed the credit until he was committed.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does the entry blame for Morton's ruin?
choix: The cost of buying the ether needed for his demonstrations
The repayment of compensation paid to the patient Abbott
A fine imposed by the hospital after the demonstration
The legal costs of his ether patent
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Morton had filed a patent on the use of ether and spent the rest of his life defending it in court. He dies in 1868, ruined by these costs, after a collapse following his reading of an article crediting Jackson with the discovery.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How fast did the discovery spread outside the United States?
choix: The first European operation had to wait until 1859
The method remained confined to Boston until Morton's death
By December 1846, European surgeons are operating under ether
Europe adopted it only after the patent dispute was settled
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The news crosses the Atlantic in a few weeks, and ether anesthesia becomes, within a season, a worldwide advance. It could be reproduced immediately by anyone with ether and an inhaler, which no patent and no quarrel over paternity could hold back.
